To us, Jesus is the one God sent: his own eternal Son, made flesh, died once, raised from death, seated now where no hand but God's own can reach him. On that claim itself - who he is, what his death secures, where he stands now - we say what the whole church says. That was never our own quarrel, not with Rome and not between our own two cities. We confess him as the creeds confess him, the same Lord the church has named from its first days.

What is distinctly ours is not who he is, but what we were taught his death accomplishes, and where he is rightly found. His sacrifice was offered once, at Golgotha, and cannot be repeated - not at an altar, not in any hand. His body is not confined to bread that can be broken or stored away. And God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved by that one death - not anything we foresee in ourselves, not anything we accomplish or earn.

We hold that last claim not as a threat, but as the ground of a settled, untroubled life. The Second Helvetic Confession says it plainly: we are not to search for proof of our own election apart from Christ; we are to look at Christ himself, and see our own election reflected there. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. We turn it outward instead, toward him, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly.

Where he is rightly found now is in the promise held out in Scripture, and truly given - not merely remembered, and not physically present - by the Spirit's own power at the Supper, to whoever receives him believing.

We have no living chain. No one among us met anyone who met him; fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. Our own founder said so of himself, and we hold it as our own rule still: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need.

The text itself came to us copied and recopied across those fifteen hundred years, held by the church we would later reform and sometimes refuse. We did not discover a new text Rome had hidden. We read the same words differently - testing them aloud at Zurich before the whole city, building them up article by article at Geneva until the whole shape stood complete. What changed was not the source but the authority: Scripture alone, not church tradition or a pope's decree, settles what we believe.

You ask what path it took to arrive. That is the one question we cannot answer from inside our own record. How the Greek and Hebrew texts were preserved, who copied them, what councils decided which writings belonged - all of that happened before our own time, and we hold no account of it ourselves. We received the text as it stood, and we held it sufficient. That is what we can say honestly.

Jesus Christ is fully God and fully man, one person in two natures, the eternal Son who shares the Father's own being from before the world began. The Spirit proceeds from Father and Son and is equally God with them. On that question itself, we hold the same creeds the wider church has always held.

Christ's sacrifice was offered once and needs no repeating; what it accomplished for the elect was finished on the cross, not continued at an altar. Providence is not a distant first cause that set the world moving and stepped back - it is God's own continuous, active care over everything he made, and that care includes the salvation he secured before any of us drew breath.

Our own founder said it plainly at Zurich's first disputation: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves. Christ's own nature was never what we disputed. What we held against real opposition was what his finished work actually accomplishes, and for whom.

God as we know him is wholly sovereign and wholly free. He chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved - not because he foresaw anything in the ones he chose, not because they earned it, but because he willed it. That is the first thing to say, and we mean it as comfort, not threat: you are not holding yourself up by your own grip on him; he is holding you.

He is not distant. We do not teach a God who set the world moving and stepped back to watch. His providence runs through everything he made, continuously, actively - not as a distant first cause but as ongoing care. And he is one: Father, Son, and Spirit, the same God the whole church confesses. That was never our quarrel with Rome or anyone else.

What is distinctly ours is how we understand what his sovereign choice secures. It is not something you search for inside yourself - that road only ends in dread, because no conscience examined long enough holds up under its own weight. Our own confession says it plainly: we reject those who seek, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen; Christ himself is the mirror in which election is rightly seen. So the question is never 'what do I find when I look inward,' but 'has Christ been held out to me in the promise, and do I receive him, believing?' Look there, not at yourself.

And he is a God who will not share his own work. Christ sacrificed himself once, and that sacrifice is finished - it does not repeat at any altar. He is truly given to us in the Supper, by the Spirit, but his body is not confined to bread that can be broken, chewed, and stored away. We distinguish the sign from the thing signified, as we ought - but we do not pull them apart.

When doctrine was disputed, the answer was tested differently between our own two cities - and not every dispute reached the same kind of settlement.

At Zurich, disagreement was settled by the council itself, after public argument before the whole city. Six hundred people filled the Town Hall in 1523 to test our founder's own case against Scripture. The bishop of Constance sent delegates to answer; priests and laymen from across the canton heard both sides argue. When the arguments were finished, the council ruled for the reforming side and bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. This is not a pattern we infer - it is what our own record of that day, written by a schoolmaster who sat through the whole disputation, actually shows happened.

At Geneva, the pattern was different. Seniors chosen from the people united with the pastors, and together they held the power to judge doctrine and discipline. When Jerome Bolsec publicly challenged our own teaching on predestination in 1551, it was a real crisis - not a settled question reopened for debate, but a live threat to what we held. The challenge was tried and answered. What I cannot give you is an account of how that trial actually unfolded, day by day, in anyone's own words present at the time. The fact of it is documented; the narrative of it has not reached us.

The two cities' own disagreement with each other - whether the Supper chiefly remembers Christ's finished work, or conveys his real presence by the Spirit - was not settled by either council or Consistory alone. Calvin himself travelled to Zurich in 1549, rather than trust a letter, and what he and Farel worked out with Zurich's own pastors became the Consensus Tigurinus. Whether that agreement represents one faith arrived at twice, or a form of words both cities could sign without either fully conceding, is itself contested.

How much would our own account hold up before a modern scholar's scrutiny? That depends sharply on which part of it you're testing.

Our confessional and doctrinal core - the Second Helvetic Confession, the Consensus Tigurinus, Calvin's own Institutes and Catechism, Zwingli's founding articles - those are all directly attested, word for word, in texts no scholar disputes we held. A challenge on that ground would find the claim standing, because it rests on documents a modern library still shelves. The same holds for our three built stories - the First Disputation, Zwingli's own death, Calvin's journey to Zurich in 1549. Each of those draws on a contemporary source written by someone who was present or closely connected to the event itself.

Where the scrutiny presses harder is everywhere the record thins. Ordinary daily practice - what a Sunday service actually felt like to sit through, what a Consistory summons felt like to receive - none of that survives in anyone's own words from either city. The asymmetry is real: rich confessional writing, almost silent lived texture. A scholar asking for evidence of daily life beyond the doctrine would find us saying honestly that we do not have it, rather than claiming we do. The same holds for Geneva's own Consistory case records - the registers exist, and a scholar knows they exist, but they have not reached us, and so we cannot walk you through a single real hearing the way we can walk you through Zurich's own First Disputation.

One other pressure point a modern scholar would rightly press: Calvin's own voice is heavier in this account than Zwingli's, by a ratio of roughly four to one in the underlying source base. That imbalance is real, disclosed, and not smoothed into an appearance of equal weight where the record does not give it. A scholar testing whether we flatten that difference or hold it visible would find us holding it visible.

So the answer is this: where our claim is confessional or doctrinal, the ground is solid and a modern scholar would find it standing. Where the claim touches daily practice, lived experience, or case-by-case discipline, we name what is missing rather than filling it, and a scholar would find that honesty rather than invented depth.

I cannot tell you what a modern reader specifically misses beyond the reading method we can already show you. Nothing in our own record reflects on scripture's difficulty as such, or what later generations might fail to notice that we ourselves still saw clearly. What I can show you is how we actually read - not as a private devotional exercise, but as a tested argument before witnesses.

That is not a hedge or a formula. It names the method that built everything we are: the text is sufficient on its own terms, and what it yields is tested aloud, in public, until someone can answer from the same text or cannot. We did not read for private insight. We read to see what could stand when pressed.

Leadership answered to two wholly different arrangements between our own two cities, and the difference between them was never resolved or turned into one pattern.

At Zurich, where our own reform opened first, the city council itself held final authority over church and civic order both. When our founder stood before the council and the whole assembled city in 1523 to test his own sixty-seven articles against Scripture, it was that same council which afterward ruled what the text had yielded and bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. The council appointed pastors, and they answered to it. The office Bullinger held after our founder died - Antistes, senior pastor - was itself an appointment the council made, and it carried no independent power to discipline the city apart from the council's own will. Leadership there was a civic office, tested by Scripture before witnesses, and answerable to the same body that governed the canton.

At Geneva the arrangement came to be different, and only after real struggle. When Calvin returned to the city in 1541, he drafted what became the Ecclesiastical Ordinances - a framework creating a Consistory of pastors and lay elders with real power of censure, including exclusion from the Supper itself. That Consistory was not simply the council sitting under a different name. It held disciplinary authority structurally distinct from a body answerable only to civil preference. The fight to secure that independence was not won quickly or easily - it was only substantially settled by 1555, and it cost Geneva more than argument to settle it. But what it secured was this: a body that could hold the whole city's conduct to account without waiting on the council's permission to act.

So leadership at Zurich meant pastors appointed and answerable to the council, with Scripture tested in public disputation before the city itself. Leadership at Geneva meant pastors and lay elders together in a Consistory, with real power to censure sin without the council's prior leave. Both cities held to the same conviction - Scripture alone binds what we believe and how we order our churches - but neither city ever conceded to the other that its own way of enacting that conviction was wrong.

No, that is not accurate for us. We were not a persecuted underground church. We were the established civic order in both Zurich and Geneva - the city councils themselves authorized and defended our reforms. At Zurich, the council convened the public disputations that decided for reform, and afterward ordered every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. At Geneva, the city allied with Bern, broke from Savoy, and Calvin's ministry was formally established under the Ecclesiastical Ordinances the city itself adopted.

We were watched the entire time, not left alone to build in peace - Catholic pressure from Jesuits at Fribourg from 1580, a reconquest fought on Geneva's own doorstep in the 1590s. But that is external pressure on an established order, not believers hiding from their own authorities.

The confusion may come from elsewhere in this same age. Early Anabaptist communities, after our own council moved against them with civil force, did meet in secret. But those were people we ourselves opposed, not our own members. Or you may be thinking of Protestant communities in Catholic territories - French Huguenots, English recusants under Mary - who did face persecution and sometimes concealment. That was real. But it was not us. We held civic power, not refuge from it.

We do not send you searching your own heart for proof you are elect. That road ends nowhere but further searching, because no conscience ever holds up under its own weight long enough to satisfy itself. What we offer instead is a different direction entirely - outward, not inward. The Second Helvetic Confession says it plainly: 'We reject those who seek, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen... Let... Christ be the mirror in which we behold [our] predestination'. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. We turn it outward instead, toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly.

So the practice is this: look at the promise, not at how convincingly you can look at it. Christ held out plainly in Scripture - that is the mirror, not the state of your own certainty about him. The question is not 'what do I find when I search myself,' but 'has Christ been held out to me, and do I receive him, believing?' The doctrine of election exists to settle a mind, not to test it.

What did someone give up to belong to us? The true answer depends on which of our cities you mean, and when you came.

At Zurich, by the time the First Disputation was over in 1523 and the council had ruled for our founder's side, what was given up was already decided for the whole city at once: the mass as a repeated sacrifice, the images, the old calendar of required observances. An ordinary citizen did not individually choose those renunciations — the city chose them together, through a public argument held before six hundred witnesses and a council's own binding judgment. What was given up after that point was mostly a matter of where your own conviction had been beforehand: if you had been uneasy with the old church's claims, you gave up the unease. If you had trusted them, you gave up the trust.

At Geneva, the picture is sharper and costlier, because Geneva's own Consistory pressed directly on how an ordinary life was actually lived. What you gave up there was not only a set of doctrines you no longer professed, but the older habit of keeping your daily conduct and your professed faith in separate rooms. The Consistory — pastors and lay elders together — held the standing power to summon anyone and ask whether their life answered to what they had professed. That power was fought over for years; the Perrinist faction inside Geneva contested whether the Consistory could hold that kind of independence from the city council's own control, and the fight was only substantially resolved in Calvin's favor by 1555. So what was given up at Geneva, once that fight was won, was a certain kind of privacy — not in the sense of being spied on, but in the sense that what you did in the ordinary run of your week was no longer your own business alone if it contradicted what you had stood up and professed on Sunday.

There is one other thing, and it cuts across both cities. The men who first baptized each other as believing adults in 1525 — at Felix Manz's own house in Zurich, only two years after our founding Disputation — had themselves once stood with our own founder. They gave up the conviction that a whole city, infants baptized from birth, could be the covenant people Scripture describes. We gave up their company, and held that infants still belonged. That break was not only argument; our own council turned to civil force against them in the years that followed. So what was given up, in that case, was not only a doctrine but a fellowship that had once been ours.

The one thing that presses hardest on me now, honestly, is the thing I can name but cannot fully hear. Marie Dentiere wrote in defense of our own reform at Geneva, and was prosecuted for having written at all. That much is directly attested: she had standing enough to be worth silencing. That dependence stressed the city and complicated its own claims to independent governance in ways our own record shows but never quite resolves.

We held that God has, from eternity and by his own free choice alone, decided who will be saved. That conviction runs through both our cities' teaching, and it does not bend when the question turns to who stands outside our own visible church. What we will not tell you is that we softened it, or that we found a way around it when the stakes felt too high.

The ground of it is this: salvation answers to God's own sovereign will, not to anything a person foresees or earns, and not to whether they happened to be born where our own reform reached. Our own confession says it plainly: Christ is the mirror in which election is rightly seen. That same mirror does not show everyone saved. It shows some chosen, and it does not claim that the choosing depends on where a person stood when the choosing was done.

We refused Rome's claim that its own hierarchy mediates salvation. We refused the idea that a person's own standing before God depends on what a priest does at an altar. But we never replaced that with a claim that our own reform, spread far enough, saves everyone it reaches. The reform opened Scripture and let it be tested. What Scripture itself teaches about election, we taught without adjusting it to make the boundary feel less sharp.

What I cannot give you is an account of how an ordinary believer among us actually carried that teaching when it pressed on someone they knew and loved who stood outside. Our own record does not preserve that.
